meaningMnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means announce .
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means chapter .
This is the comb radical. Look at all those little things sticking out. You could easily use this to comb your hair.

This is the droopy radical because it looks like a droopy ice cream cake on a stand. Melty goodness droops over the edge of each layer, and the whole top section is drooping toward the left like it's about to give in to gravity. Imagine how melted it must be for it to be so droopy… better eat it quick.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means ten thousand .

This is the warehouse radical. Do you see the roof with all the shelving units underneath? There's even a ladder to help you reach the taller shelves. Imagine all the things you could store in your warehouse.

Your fingers touch as you stand with a woman and adjoin yourselves. You are united, you are one. Hints Look around you. Other women are adjoining their fingers and standing with you. There's hundreds, no, thousands of you standing together.
readingMnemonic: All the women adjoin in sets ( せつ ). Sets of two, of course. One woman with another woman, standing in unison. Hints Picture a bunch of women standing together. They're holding hands in sets, adjoined together.

meaningMnemonic: Under the ground , a head covered in dirt emerges... again ! It's not the first time you've seen this buried head, nor is it the last. This dirt-covered head hides beneath the ground wherever you go, and keeps popping up to scare you again and again. Hints Picture the dirt-covered head popping up again and again. How can it move under the ground like that if it's just a head? You decide to get closer this time, and for once it speaks: "Get me out of the ground!"
readingMnemonic: The dirt-covered head asks for help again and again, but you've only got a saw ( さ ). So you start digging with it, scraping the dirt away, until you see this head has the body of a cy borg ( さい )! Hints Imagine how dirty you and your saw are after all this. At least you could help this cyborg with your saw. "Thanks again," it says, then runs off shaking the dirt out of its hair.

meaningMnemonic: There once was an animal with an insect friend who felt very alone unless he was around. An animal and an insect are an unlikely pairing, but these two get along delightfully and hate to be alone without the other. Hints Imagine this animal and this insect. Let’s say it’s a flea and a dog. Imagine them going everywhere together. To the park, getting ice cream, even the drive in movie theater. They’re inseparable.
readingMnemonic: One activity that the animal can never do alone is solve Su doku ( どく ) puzzles. The insect always has to help him out with them, and together they are an unstoppable Sudoku solving team. Hints Picture this animal with the insect on his head doing a Sudoku. See the insect hopping around on the animals head shouting answers and suggestions into the animal’s ear. How cute.

meaningMnemonic: On the grass near a rice paddy sits a creeper that is some sort of a dog beast , a vicious animal . This creeper isn’t just a normal dog, it is more beast-like, more like a feral animal than domesticated pet. Hints Picture this beast creeping, low to the ground, in the grass around the rice paddy. It's got its eyes on you. Uh oh.
readingMnemonic: The beast is guarding its precious jew els ( じゅう ), which it buried in the grass or the rice paddy somewhere. If you don't want the beast to think you're coming to steal those jewels, you better keep your distance. Hints All beasts have something they're trying to protect. In this case, it's some beastly jewels.

meaningMnemonic: You take some flowers and some fruit and you make a cake out of it. It’s a very nice looking, flavorful cake. The fruit makes it taste great and the flowers make for great cake decorations. Hints Look at this cake you have made. It’s majestic. Now taste some of it. It is one great tasting cake. Imagine yourself eating the best cake in all of ever.
readingMnemonic: You’re standing back, admiring your cake when you hear a ca r ( か ) engine revving and before you know it your cake has been run over. The car came out of nowhere and ran your cake right over, spraying fruit cake bits and flowers all over the place. Stupid car! Hints Hear the roar of the car engine as you get splattered in the face with the cake. Wipe it off of your face just in time to see the car speeding off into the distance. Also, recall that this kanji shares a reading with the similar kanji, 果 .

meaningMnemonic: They say using a measurement device (like a ruler) is a good way to chastise someone. They do something bad? Chastise them by slapping their wrists, their feet, their eyes, ears, anything! They say something out of turn? CHASTISE THEM! Hints Imagine being chastised with a measurement device. Think how horrible it would be getting hit on your knuckles, your nose, or the back of your head. It would be awful. Imagine this experience.
readingMnemonic: You're being chastise d because you tried to say something in English in とう きょう . Everyone around you slowly turned around, eyes aflame and rulers in hand, ready to chastise you for uttering those forbidden words. Hints How could you say something in English while you're in とうきょう ?! After you went to all the trouble to learn all this kanji and Japanese? Geez, we almost think you deserve to be chastised...

meaningMnemonic: The old winter is to blame for today's circumstance . It is the reason things are bad now. Hints Imagine a poor, broken town. And, imagine the mayor of a town telling their people that things are bad because of that bad old winter. "It's to blame for our circumstance!" he yells.
readingMnemonic: In reality, this circumstance was actually caused by a single 子 ( こ ), though. This kid went through town, destroying everything in their path. Hints Imagine your kid character walking through town, using their super powers to destroy buildings and rot food.

meaningMnemonic: Your new car doesn’t mix well with the other cars in your garage because its color is in stark contrast to the others. All of your other cars are pristine white in color, but this new car is a mix of lots of colors. It almost looks like a peacock or something it’s so colorful. Such a contrast. Hints Imagine this garage of yours with a sea of white cars. Now there is a new car that really sticks out like a sore thumb. Imagine yourself looking out over your cars and seeing this wacky car practically jumping out at you.
readingMnemonic: What did I say this car looks like? Oh that’s right, a pea cock ( かく ). This car looks like a peacock. It’s the color of a peacock and you’ll look like you’re peacocking when you’re out on the town driving it. It really is such a stark contrast to like, every other car out there. Hints See yourself driving around in this peacock car. Hear the engine purr as strangers jeer and yell at you. This car sure does get a lot of attention, doesn’t it?

meaningMnemonic: In your warehouse you use your knife to create . You keep old pieces of wood in your warehouse, and you use your knife to carve them into new things that only you could create. Hints What do you create in your warehouse? Picture all the different things you could create in your mind.
readingMnemonic: When you create it's good for your sou l ( そう ). It's so freeing, in fact, that when you get really into your creating, sometimes you'd swear your soul was floating a little bit outside of your body. But every time you notice, it sinks back down. Hmm. Hints When you create something your soul is happy! It's good for you, you know?

meaningMnemonic: "A scooter !" you announce . You are announcing this because you decided this is what you would create . Hints Imagine being at a maker's contest. Each person has to announce loudly what they'll create, then they have to create it.
readingMnemonic: But, a scooter has been create d before. What is different about yours? The scooter you will create is specifically designed to keep zo mbies ( ぞう ) busy. Hints Imagine the scooter you created with a zombie on it. It's a perfect place for the zombie to get stuck and scooted off into nowhere.

meaningMnemonic: This kanji comes straight from the droopy radical. What do droopy things do? They droop . Oh, and sometimes they dangle too. Hints Don't let your spirits droop — kanji can be tough to learn, but you're doing great!
readingMnemonic: You know what's better when it droop s a little? A swi ng ( すい ). Those swings with the droopy rubber seats are so comfortable to sit on and dangle your legs off of — way better than the rigid wooden ones. Hints Imagine setting your bum in a droopy rubber swing seat. Feel it droop down a little lower as you put your weight into it and let your legs dangle. Ah, such comfort.

meaningMnemonic: The " Cliff of Ten Thousand Power " is where you go if you want to be encourage d. Hints If you can get to the top of the cliff, it will use its "ten thousand power" to encourage you.
readingMnemonic: When you get there, it does encourage you. The cliff says "Hey, I encourage you to buy a ray ( れい ) gun." Hints A cliff is encouraging you to buy a ray gun for some reason. This is not the encouragement you expected, but it is encouragement nonetheless. You go back down the cliff and immediately buy a ray gun.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami that is white , traveling in the direction of winter is a fierce and violent force of nature. This white tsunami is chasing after winter, and that’s why the tsunami is white—it’s a winter tsunami. It’s the most fierce and most violent kind of tsunami in existence. Hints Imagine this white tsunami, more violent and fierce than any other tsunami you’ve ever seen, coming toward you. It’s very frightening. Feel the cold wetness it brings to your skin.
readingMnemonic: The tsunami is too fierce , too violent , and before you realize what's happening, Gecki ( げき ), your beloved gecko, is lifted up and carried off into the air. Hints "Geecckkkiiiiii!!!" you scream in horror, as he's thrown about by the fierce, winter tsunami. You have to close your eyes. You can't watch Gecki go.

meaningMnemonic: This flag marks where people used to loiter until a black hole swallowed them up, leaving behind only their footwear . Hints Imagine coming across this flag that memorializes the loiterers. You hear it flapping in the wind and wonder: Why did a black hole appear so suddenly here? Those poor, poor loiterers. Sucked right out of their footwear.
readingMnemonic: When you look closer, it turns out the loiterers had all been wearing footwear made of ree ds ( り ). Makes sense, since a loiterer's laidback lifestyle is perfectly suited for reed footwear. Hints Now take this rough, reed footwear in your hands. Caress it as if trying to conjure a genie out of a lamp — though your only wish is to know what happened here.

meaningMnemonic: The fortune radical and the fortune kanji are exactly the same! This can also mean occupy , maybe because learning your fortune shows you how you're going to occupy your life. Or how it will occupy you… You haven't seen the radical in a while, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember the kanji: Put your toe in your mouth to learn your fortune . The taste will tell you everything you need to know about your fortune. But your toe has to occupy your mouth first for it to work. Hints Imagine what your toe tastes like. Or actually taste it, I don't care. What do the taste and texture of it say about you, about your future fortune?
readingMnemonic: To occupy some free time you have, you go and get your fortune told at a fortune teller. Your fortune is that you’ll have an encounter with a cen taur ( せん ) in the near future. Just then you realize that the fortune teller is actually a centaur! The fortune has come true! Hints Imagine getting your fortune told by a centaur fortune teller. Do you trust this mythical beast to know your future? Watch him manipulate his crystal ball as his hooves stomp the ground beneath him.

meaningMnemonic: There's a building standing in the way of the next chapter in your life, and it's hinder ing you. It's not like you couldn't find another way around, but it's definitely inconvenient. Hints Picture this huge, tall building standing directly in the way. You peer around the other side and there is a book floating in the air that says "Chapter 5: Success and Happiness." Dang, you really want to get over there to that part of your life.
readingMnemonic: Someone put this building here specifically to hinder you. They knew you were close to the next chapter of your life, and they wanted to hinder you really good. And there they are, sitting on a throne smirking. It's the Shou gun ( しょう ). Hints The Shougun wants to hinder you and your life. He wants you to have to work harder so you become better, faster, and stronger than anyone else. Hindering you is his way of making sure you don't take the easy way out in life.

meaningMnemonic: Your ego ... it's totally out of control. I mean, my ego isn't out of control. I'm the greatest. That's me . But your ego? Ugh, so out of control unlike my amazing ego. Hints Just keep going with this sentence about the ego. You can't stop, because really it's your ego that's out of control. That's I when you're saying it.
readingMnemonic: I am the greatest in the world! I am no baby like you, that's why. A baby who says " ga ( が ) ga ga ga!" Hints You're just destroying the ego of that other guy. "Why?" you ask? "Because I am the boss here. And you are the baby. Ego things."

meaningMnemonic: A loiter ing mountain king in the winter is an indication or sign of something to come. Hints We don't want to focus too much on what the indication / sign actually is, though, because it will take away from the indication part (which we want to remember). So, focus on the fact that this is some kind of indication that's important, but you don't know what that indication means or is... because we'll use that with the reading.
readingMnemonic: When you spot a loitering mountain king in the winter, you know it's an indication that soon Mrs. Chou ( ちょう ) will appear. It's like a Groundhog's Day kind of situation, but instead it means Mrs. Chou is about to come out, perhaps early for the season. Hints Imagine an announcer watching the loitering mountain king, "There he is... and it's still winter. We all know what that means. It's a sign that Mrs. Chou will be coming out of hibernation soon." Then, you can imagine her bursting forth from the mountain, running down her street.

meaningMnemonic: There are fingers reaching towards you asking you to accept to instruct them. They're the fingers of students. And you're the teacher. See them reach out for knowledge. They want to accept this knowledge into their hearts and brains. Instruct them! Hints Picture yourself instructing a class full of knowledge hungry little kids. They reach out with their fingers to accept the truth you bring to them.
readingMnemonic: "Yes! I will instruct you, my dear students!" you cry, "I will instruct you on how to open a small ju ice ( じゅ ) box!" That's right. These little kids need help learning how to open small juice boxes (small because kids are small). Hints Picture yourself instructing little kids how to punch the straw into small juice boxes. Hold it right-side-up! Don't squeeze too hard! Don't punch it through the other side! No! Don't bite the box! Instructing is hard!

meaningMnemonic: You loiter around your master until he depart s on a journey . You have a lot more freedom to do things after your master has departed, so until that time you just loiter about looking busy and staying out of his way. Hints Picture yourself loitering around your master’s fancy mansion. You’re pretending to dust things off, but you’re actually just waiting for him to depart on his journey.
readingMnemonic: Finally, it's time for your master's journey and he calls to you and says, "You are the 王 ( おう ) of the house now. Take care of everything while I'm gone." Hints Your master has departed! You are the 王 now!

meaningMnemonic: You hold gold fins in your mouth while shopping for pencil lead at the store. This pencil lead store only accepts gold fins as payment, but your fins don’t fit in your pockets and you need your hands to carry the lead so the gold fins go in your mouth. Hints Imagine having these gold fins in your mouth. Taste the metal as your tongue runs over them.
readingMnemonic: You pay for your lead but the cashier puts it in your mouth where the gold fins were and... everything en ds ( えん ). Hints Lead poisoning, huh? What a way for everything to end...

meaningMnemonic: The droopy building is where people droop under big sacks of mail , aka a post office. Hints Picture a bunch of postal workers going in and out of the post office building, drooping under the weight of so much mail. It's a tough job.
readingMnemonic: Because it's such a physically demanding job, all the mail carriers in this post office are you ths ( ゆう ). Only the youths can handle this kind of heavy mail-bag lifting, I guess. Hints Imagine all these droopy youths, showing up for the morning shift to pay their way through college as mail carriers. Ah, you were one of them once…

meaningMnemonic: In a gold cross , you see a needle sticking out of it. The needle is right in the middle of the gold cross. If Jesus were on there, the needle would be sticking him right in the chest. Hints Picture this golden cross in your head. Why do you suppose there’s this needle stuck in it? You try to pull it out but you can’t. Envision yourself straining, trying to get the thing out.
readingMnemonic: You're about to give up on the needle when it pops out and flies directly into your shin ( しん ). Ouch! Now you're desperately trying to pull the needle out of your shin, but it really won't budge this time. Maybe you should have minded your own business. Hints Imagine a needle sticking into your shin. It hurts a ton. How would you try to get it out?

meaningMnemonic: If you see some entity loiter ing with horns on its head atop your coat rack , you should probably obey it and accompany it wherever it leads you. Hints First of all, this could be really fun. Second of all, if this entity is a demon or something, you should really just obey it or it might curse you. What's the worst that could happen?!
readingMnemonic: If you obey the horned entity atop your coat rack, you'll end up with a ton of jew els ( じゅう )! Hints Pledging to obey and accompany a mysterious horned entity who lavishes jewels upon you definitely seems like a good decision. Not sketchy at all.

meaningMnemonic: During a tsunami , your lip ring is ripped off while you’re trying to cross a river . There was no other path to safety, you had to cross the raging river, but you lost your footing and smashed your face on a rock and lost your lip ring. Hints Imagine how painful this would be, having your lip ring ripped from your lip. It would hurt a lot. Touch your lip and imagine missing half of it. Yikes.
readingMnemonic: But why were you trying to cross this river anyway? Well your ca r ( か ) was on the other side of it, and you figured if you could get to your car you could outrun the tsunami and be safe. Too bad you fell and ripped out your lip ring though. Hints Imagine yourself fording the river, all wet and cold from the water. Keeping your eyes on your car, you move slowly across. Look at the car. Look at it!

meaningMnemonic: You keep all of your shellfish under a roof down the street and it's your savings . Shellfish used to be used as money way back, and these aren't shellfish you're spending, they're ones you're saving up for later. Hints Imagine walking down the street to deposit more shellfish into your special savings and gaze happily at the huge pile you keep far enough away that you aren't tempted to spend it.
readingMnemonic: When you want to withdraw from your savings you force yourself to use cho psticks ( ちょ ) to pick up the shellfish. They're especially slippery, hard to use chopsticks too, that way it's really hard to take too much out of your savings. Hints Imagine trying to lift up a shellfish with a pair of smooth chopsticks. It slips right out. Ugh! I guess that's good though, because it's a savings for a reason (you shouldn't be spending it)!

meaningMnemonic: You take this comb , break the handle off, and use it to stamp your official seal of approval onto a document. It's kind of a messy mark ing process, but it gets the job done. Hints Imagine breaking and bending a comb so you can use it to stamp your seal onto things.
readingMnemonic: You need this seal to stay at an inn ( いん ). All inns require official paperwork, so you had to improvise and make a seal on the fly. Hints Hopefully the inn accepts this seal... or you aren't going to have a place to sleep tonight. And it kind of just looks like you dipped a comb in ink and pressed it around on some paper.

meaningMnemonic: You're trying to use your fingers to cause a landslide so you have to shake the earth. You probably won't succeed, but the best you can do is to shake your hands on the dirt as hard as you can. It looks like you're trying to wave at the ground now. Hints Imagine shaking your fingers at the dirt. Do you think you can shake the dirt hard enough to cause a landslide (spoilers, no).
readingMnemonic: You think you finally got the earth to shake but when you look down it's just your shin s ( しん ). Darn you shins, I thought I made some progress. Hey wait... why won't you stop?! Hints Imagine your shins shaking, your hands are waving, and they won't stop. No! You shouldn't have tried to start a landslide. This was a bad idea!

meaningMnemonic: When you hold out your fingers , a person — and then a second person — stomps them into the dirt , leaving you with a serious finger sprain . That wasn't very nice of either person, and now you feel awfully discourage d about things. Hints Feel the throbbing pain in your sprained, dirt-covered fingers, and imagine how intensely discouraged you are knowing that neither person who hurt you is going to face any consequences.
readingMnemonic: You show your sprain to a doctor, and he tells you to go see the C za r ( ざ ). In your country, only the Czar has the authority to treat a sprain of this severity. Hints Once again, you face a crushing sense of discouragement — you'll never be able to afford the services of the Czar! It looks you're just going to have to live with this finger sprain for the rest of your life.

meaningMnemonic: You see a soul floating around a tombstone acting suspicious . To be fair, if a soul is going to be anywhere, a tombstone is probably high up on the list, but this one seems like it's doing something weird. Hints Imagine inching closer to this suspicious soul floating around a tombstone. What do you think it's doing?
readingMnemonic: You sneak around the tombstone to see what this suspicious soul is doing, and you realize it's pretending to kay ak ( かい ). The soul is sitting behind the tombstone, in a small kayak, moving its arms like it's rowing through water. Even more suspicious, the soul seems to be holding a ke ttle ( け ). Considering the soul is already dead, this doesn't seem like something it will need. Hints Picture a suspicious, kettle holding, kayaking soul. The afterlife may be more interesting than you thought.

meaningMnemonic: The tsunami going down your dry face is just sweat . Hints Sweat really does feel like a tsunami though. Wow, it's dry and hot out right now!
readingMnemonic: The sweat isn't just on your face, it's also dripping down your ass ( あせ ). Hints The one place you wish sweat wouldn't go, but somehow it always does: the ass.

meaningMnemonic: "Take your fingers . Now , put them on your foe's heart and twist ." These are the words of your martial arts master as he teaches you his final, ultimate technique: the "finger-heart twister." Hints No one can stop you now. Imagine how powerful you feel as you conquer dojo after dojo, using your bare fingers to twist the heart of any challenger who dares face you. What a twisted fiend you are!
readingMnemonic: The last challenger to appear is… your own master, who taught you the twist technique. Turns out he's a nen doroid ( ねん ) — one of those cute, plastic anime figurines — so he doesn't even have a heart for you to twist. Welp, you're screwed. Hints Imagine the helplessness you'd feel facing him. Your master, who all along was a nendoroid, is impervious to the twist technique he himself taught you! What a twist.

meaningMnemonic: You're using your fingers to do something important for this ceremony 's construction . What's really important for this ceremony's construction, using your fingers? Well… you wipe the floors. Hints Hey, somebody has to do it! Wiping the floors is as important for any ceremony as all the other work that goes into it… right?!
readingMnemonic: Now wipe these floors, you foo l ( ふ )! Hints Oh wow, sorry, not sure where that just came from… Look, wiping floors for a living doesn't make anyone a fool, they're people just like you and me. Now hurry up, I want a nice sheen on these floors before the ceremony.

meaningMnemonic: Out of bamboo , you make a brush – a writing brush . This is no ordinary brush, mind you. It is a brush specifically designed for writing elegant characters. And it’s made from bamboo! Hints Imagine yourself using this bamboo writing brush. Do you know many kanji? Of course you do! Imagine yourself writing them all with this nice writing brush. It’s actually fun to write things with it!
readingMnemonic: Once the writing brush hits ( ひつ ) that paper, it’s like you transform into a totally different person. All of a sudden you’re a master calligrapher, writing anything and everything in a most beautiful fashion. Once that brush hits the paper, it’s on! Hints Imagine the sound the brush makes when it hits the paper. It’s a bit of a plop, and then kind of a scratching sound as the brush bristles move around. Really focus on this sound that the brush makes when it hits the paper.

meaningMnemonic: An occurrence that only results because of circumstance s is also called an accident . You didn't want this bad thing to happen, it was just an occurrence of circumstance! Everything aligned in the worst way. 事故 is mostly used to refer to physical accidents, like traffic accidents ( 交通事故 ) or construction accidents ( 建設事故 ). Sometimes other kinds of mishap s get the 事故 label too, like broadcast mishaps ( 放送事故 ), where something inappropriate or unplanned happens on air.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 王子を船で川の向こう岸へ渡していた時に、事故が起きたんです。
sentences.english: When I was ferrying the prince across the river by boat to the opposite bank, an accident occurred.

sentences.japanese: 車を買ってまだ半年しかたっていないのに、もう事故に巻きこまれてしまった。
sentences.english: I had only owned the car for half a year, and I already got involved in an accident.

sentences.japanese: ひき逃げ事故のせいで、買ったばかりの牛肉が挽き肉になった。
sentences.english: Due to the hit-and-run accident, the beef he just bought became ground beef.

meaningMnemonic: Again with that occurrence ? That occurrence has now happened again . Note that this word is relatively formal.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just remember that there's a い hiding in there!

sentences.japanese: この件については再度検討した方がいいかもね。
sentences.english: Perhaps we should look into this again.

sentences.japanese: 計画は再度たな上げになってしまった。
sentences.english: The project was shelved for the second time.

sentences.japanese: お手数ですが、念のため再度確認していただけないでしょうか。
sentences.english: I’m sorry to trouble you, but could you please check again to be sure?

sentences.japanese: 相手は、埋め立て計画に反対する請願書を再度持ってくるかもしれませんよ。
sentences.english: They may bring forward a petition against our land reclamation project again.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. While 一人 simply means "one person," 独り carries a stronger sense of being alone , often with connotations of solitude . It can also mean someone is single (as in not married).
readingMnemonic: The reading is different from the one you learned (this is kun'yomi). There's an easy way to remember it, though. 一人 and 独り share the same readings and mean almost the same thing. Just try to remember that this ひとり is used to emphasize solitude.

sentences.japanese: 全てを失って、独りぼっちになってしまった。
sentences.english: After losing everything, I ended up all alone.

sentences.japanese: これからずっと独りで生きなくちゃいけないのか。
sentences.english: It seems like I have to live alone from now on.

sentences.japanese: 彼も独りで住んでいるよ。
sentences.english: He lives alone too.

meaningMnemonic: We waited an interval of time , and at each interval it was different . They're all supposed to be the same. Is there some kind of mistake ?
readingMnemonic: Take the reading of 間 ( ま from 間に合う ) and 違う and you'll have the reading for this word too.

sentences.japanese: 間違いを一つ見つけたよ！
sentences.english: I found one mistake!

sentences.japanese: これは間違いないね！
sentences.english: This is unmistakable, isn't it?

sentences.japanese: ファイナルファンタジーについて君に聞いたのが間違いだったよ。
sentences.english: It was a mistake to ask you about Final Fantasy.

sentences.japanese: 新しい市場に参入したことは間違いじゃなかった。
sentences.english: Expanding into new markets was not a mistake.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember: A beast ... what do you think of when you think of a beast? How about a thing ( 物 , もの ) full of fur ( 毛 , け ), aka a けもの (fur thing)? A beast is a fur thing, and in Japanese that's けもの . Punnnns.

sentences.japanese: 獣がワナにかかったぞ！
sentences.english: The beast was caught in the trap!

sentences.japanese: 森に大きな獣が一匹住んでいる。
sentences.english: A large beast lives in the forest.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means replace , and this word means to be replaced , to be substituted , and to be switched . Wondering about the difference between 代わる and 替わる ? 代わる is used when someone or something takes the place of another, like filling in for a sick coworker. Whereas 替わる is used when things or situations switch places or are replaced with something new, like when talking about generations changing or a new governmental cabinet taking over. This verb is intransitive, meaning it doesn't take a direct object. You'll sometimes see it with the particle を , though, because the を is showing a "path" rather than a direct object in this case. For example, 席を替わる (to switch seats) indicates your location is moving from one seat to another. Likewise, 電話を替わる indicates that a call is being handed off to another person.

meaningMnemonic: 触る means "to touch," and 触れる also means to touch . The word also means to touch on , as in touching on some subject. It's still used in phrases like "When I touched your hand," but has a lighter, more indirect and literary feel than 触る , which conveys a greater sense of purpose and intent behind the action. 触れる is often used in constructions like 手がカバンに触れる (one's hand touches a bag), where が indicates what's doing the touching and に marks what's being touched.
